name: Contractualism
aliases: What We Owe to Each Other
statement: An act is wrong if it violates a principle no one could reasonably reject as a basis for shared agreement.
meaning: Contractualism is a family of moral theories holding that the morality of actions or principles is grounded in agreement, or in what people could justify to one another, and the term is especially associated with the philosopher T. M. Scanlon. Broadly, contractualism belongs to the social contract tradition in ethics, but it is important to distinguish it from Hobbesian contractarianism, associated with David Gauthier, which grounds morality in mutual advantage among rational, self-interested agents. Contractualism in the narrow, Kantian sense grounds morality instead in justifiability to others. Scanlon's version, set out in his 1998 book What We Owe to Each Other, offers a formula for wrongness: an act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behavior that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced, general agreement. On this view, the domain of right and wrong, of what we owe to each other, is a matter of acting on principles that others could not reasonably reject, so that morality is fundamentally about justifiability to others rather than about maximizing good outcomes or serving mutual advantage. Contractualism is a Kantian, non-consequentialist theory that emphasizes reasons and the distinct standpoints of individuals, and it is a major contemporary approach in normative ethics.
mechanism: Scanlon's contractualism determines the rightness and wrongness of actions by asking whether they could be justified to everyone affected. The core idea is that morality, in the sense of what we owe to each other, is the system of principles for the general regulation of behavior that no one could reasonably reject. To assess an act, one asks whether it would be permitted by such principles: an act is wrong just in case it is disallowed by any principle that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced, general agreement. The test is one of reasonable rejection, not of mutual advantage, which distinguishes contractualism from Hobbesian contractarianism; the parties are imagined not as self-interested bargainers but as people motivated by the desire to find principles others could also accept. Reasonable grounds for rejecting a principle come from the standpoints of distinct individuals, not from any collective or impersonal point of view, so objections must be raised by particular persons and cannot be pooled or aggregated in the way utilitarianism aggregates welfare. This individual-standpoint feature builds in a form of respect for the separateness of persons. Contractualism thus explains morality as a matter of acting on principles justifiable to each person, capturing the Kantian idea of treating people as ends by requiring that our conduct be defensible to them by reasons they could not reasonably reject.

examples.text: An act is wrong if it is disallowed by any principle for regulating behavior that no one could reasonably reject.

Objections to a principle come from distinct individuals and cannot be aggregated as utilitarianism aggregates welfare.

variants.name: Contractualism versus contractarianism
variants.text: The Kantian reasonable-rejection view of Scanlon and Rawls, versus the Hobbesian mutual-advantage view of Gauthier.

variants.name: Reasonable rejection
variants.text: The central test that a principle is justified if no individual could reasonably reject it as a basis for general agreement.

whyItMatters: Contractualism is a major contemporary theory in normative ethics, offering a distinctive and influential account of morality as grounded in justifiability to others. By holding that an act is wrong if it violates any principle that no one could reasonably reject, T. M. Scanlon captured a powerful moral intuition, that morality is fundamentally about being able to justify our conduct to those affected by it, and gave it a precise formulation in his landmark book What We Owe to Each Other. Contractualism provides a compelling alternative to both consequentialism, which it rejects for focusing only on outcomes, and traditional deontology, by deriving moral principles from a procedure of reasonable agreement rather than from a fixed list of duties. Its insistence that objections must come from the standpoints of distinct individuals, blocking the aggregation of welfare across persons, offers a principled response to the utilitarian worry about sacrificing individuals for the greater good, honoring the separateness of persons. Contractualism connects ethics to the Kantian ideas of respect for persons and treating others as ends, and it has been enormously influential in moral and political philosophy.

working.text: take a principle for the general regulation of behavior that would permit or forbid the act in question.
ask whether any individual could reasonably reject that principle as a basis for informed, unforced general agreement.
count the act wrong if it is disallowed by any principle no one could reasonably reject.

limits: Contractualism is influential but faces real objections. A circularity or redundancy worry holds that the test of reasonable rejection may presuppose prior moral notions, since what counts as a reasonable ground for rejecting a principle seems to depend on independent moral judgments, so the theory may assume the very wrongness it aims to define. A scope problem arises over beings who cannot participate in the imagined agreement, such as non-human animals and future generations, to whom we seem to have moral duties that a theory grounded in justifiability to others has trouble accommodating. And an aggregation problem is pressed against contractualism's refusal to sum objections across persons, since in some cases, such as saving many people rather than one, that refusal can seem to yield counterintuitive results, and whether contractualism can properly handle numbers is debated. The distinction from Hobbesian contractarianism must also be kept clear.
misreadings: Contractualism in Scanlon's sense is not the same as Hobbesian contractarianism; it grounds morality in reasonable agreement and justifiability to others, not in mutual advantage among self-interested agents. It is not consequentialist, since it derives principles from what no one could reasonably reject rather than from maximizing good outcomes. And it does not aggregate welfare across persons, since objections come from distinct individuals, so treating contractualism as a mutual-advantage theory, as consequentialist, or as summing welfare, misreads Scanlon's account of what we owe to each other.
origin: A family of moral theories, especially T. M. Scanlon's, set out in his 1998 book What We Owe to Each Other, grounding morality in principles that no one could reasonably reject; a Kantian alternative to consequentialism and to Hobbesian contractarianism.
